mods.name: Prompting & Structured Outputs
mods.lede: The cheapest, highest-leverage skill in agent engineering: tell the model clearly what to do, show it well-chosen examples, force its output into a shape your code can trust, repair what still goes wrong, and keep prompts under test.

mods.name: Agent Architectures
mods.lede: Before choosing tools, evals or infrastructure, decide how much freedom the model gets: a fixed code path, a loop it steers, a plan it writes first, a critic it answers to, a tree it searches, a budget it thinks within, or a person who approves the risky steps.

mods.name: Tools & MCP
mods.lede: An agent is only as reliable as its tools: how a model calls them, how to design them, how to run them in parallel and retry them safely, how to find the right one among hundreds, and the open protocols that share tools and agents across applications.

mods.name: Memory & Context
mods.lede: An agent knows only what is in its context window right now, so every long-running agent needs a policy for what goes in, what gets summarized, what is saved, which proven routines are reused, and what is forgotten.

mods.name: Multi-Agent Systems
mods.lede: More agents buy breadth and speed at a steep token price, so decide whether to split first, then choose how agents coordinate, share, check each other and stop.

mods.name: Embeddings
mods.lede: Embeddings decide what your agent can find.

mods.name: Vector Databases
mods.lede: A vector database trades a little recall for a lot of speed.

mods.name: RAG Pipelines
mods.lede: Retrieval-augmented generation is a pipeline, and it fails at its weakest step.

mods.name: Evaluation
mods.lede: You can't improve an agent you can't measure.

mods.name: Guardrails
mods.lede: Guardrails decide what reaches the model, what leaves it, and what the agent is allowed to do.

mods.name: Agent Security
mods.lede: Guardrails teach the defences; this module teaches how attackers think.

mods.name: Cost Optimisation
mods.lede: Agent bills grow fast because agents loop, resend long prompts and default to the biggest model.

mods.name: Performance
mods.lede: Agents feel slow for three reasons: they take too many steps, each model call waits on prefill and token-by-token decoding, and tool calls run one after another.

mods.name: Fine-Tuning
mods.lede: Changing a model’s weights is powerful, costly and often unnecessary.

mods.name: Governance & Compliance
mods.lede: A demo becomes a product when compliance signs it off.

mods.name: Choosing a Framework
mods.lede: “Which framework should we use?” is the first question every team asks.

mods.name: Computer-Use & Voice Agents
mods.lede: Agents are learning to see screens, click through apps and hold spoken conversations.

techs.name: System-Level Eval
techs.q: Did the agent get the job done?
techs.remember: Score the outcome, count the cost, repeat the run.
techs.what: Treat the agent as a black box.

techs.name: Process-Level Eval
techs.q: Where exactly did it go wrong?
techs.remember: Grade the path, not just the destination.
techs.what: Open the black box and score the trajectory: the plan, each tool call and its arguments, the order of steps, and how the agent recovered from errors.

techs.name: LLM-as-a-Judge
techs.q: Is this output actually good?
techs.remember: Rubric first, reasoning before score, calibrate against humans.
techs.what: A strong model grades outputs against a written rubric.

techs.name: Agent-as-a-Judge
techs.q: Does the work really meet the spec?
techs.remember: Don’t just read the work. Inspect it and run it.
techs.what: The judge is itself an agent.

techs.name: RAG Grounding Metrics
techs.q: Is the answer backed by the sources?
techs.remember: Found the right context? Stayed inside it?
techs.what: Split retrieval-augmented generation into its two halves.

techs.name: Benchmark Suites
techs.q: How does it compare with the field?
techs.remember: Benchmarks to choose, private evals to ship.
techs.what: Public benchmark suites measure general agent capability on standard tasks with fixed harnesses.

techs.name: Eval Datasets
techs.q: Is the test set itself worth trusting?
techs.remember: Real cases, every slice, two labellers, enough n, and refresh from failures.
techs.what: Build and maintain the set of cases every other evaluation runs on.

techs.name: User Simulation for Multi-Turn Agents
techs.q: Does the agent still work when the user talks back?
techs.remember: An LLM plays the user; check the end state; repeat and report pass^k.
techs.what: A single-turn test gives the agent everything at once.

techs.name: Pairwise Comparison and Statistical Significance
techs.q: Is version B really better, or is it noise?
techs.remember: Same questions, both orders, a win rate with an interval; ship only if it clears 50%.
techs.what: When two versions of a prompt, model or agent are compared, the question is not “what score did B get” but “how often is B better than A on the same inputs, and could that be chance”.

techs.name: Input Guardrails
techs.q: Should this input reach the model at all?
techs.remember: Screen it early, treat untrusted text as data.
techs.what: Checks on user input, retrieved documents and tool results before they reach the model.

techs.name: PII Detection and Redaction
techs.q: Which personal data must never reach the model or the logs?
techs.remember: Detect with checksums, replace with placeholders, keep the real values short-lived.
techs.what: Finds personal data in text before it reaches a model, a log or another system, and replaces it with typed placeholders such as <IN_PAN_1>.

techs.name: Output Guardrails
techs.q: Is this response safe and true enough to send?
techs.remember: Check the draft before anyone sees it.
techs.what: Checks on the model’s draft before it reaches the user or triggers an action.

techs.name: Choosing Deterministic or Model-Based Checks
techs.q: Should a rule or a classifier catch this?
techs.remember: Rules for shapes, classifiers for meaning, rules first.
techs.what: Every guardrail is either a rule written in code or a model that judges meaning.

techs.name: Action Policies and Approval Thresholds
techs.q: Is the agent allowed to take this action, right now?
techs.remember: Deny by default, scope every call, set the approval line in code.
techs.what: Controls on what the agent does, not only what it says.

techs.name: Grounding and Hallucination Checks
techs.q: Does the retrieved text actually support what the answer says?
techs.remember: Split into claims, check each against the context, tune the threshold on labels.
techs.what: A grounding check verifies, after generation, that each claim in an answer is supported by the context it was given.

techs.name: Model Routing and Tiering
techs.q: Does this request need the big model?
techs.remember: Smallest model that passes, per request and per step. Escalate on doubt.
techs.what: Pick the cheapest model that passes, per request at run time and per pipeline step at design time.

techs.name: Prompt Caching
techs.q: Am I paying again for the same prompt prefix?
techs.remember: Static first, variable last.
techs.what: Providers can store the processed form of a long, unchanging prompt prefix, such as the system prompt, tool definitions and reference documents, and reuse it on the next call.

techs.name: Prompt & Tool Controls
techs.q: Is the agent using more tokens and calls than it needs?
techs.remember: Budget every loop. Trim every payload.
techs.what: Put limits and lean defaults on what each request can consume: concise system prompts, capped output length, fewer and tighter tool definitions, compact tool results, and a cap on how many steps an agent loop can take.

techs.name: Context Pruning
techs.q: Does the model need everything in the context window?
techs.remember: Every token is paid for on every turn.
techs.what: Long-running agents pile up history, tool output and retrieved documents, and every token is paid for again on every turn.

techs.name: Request Scheduling
techs.q: Does this have to run now, and at full speed?
techs.remember: Urgent now. Everything else when it’s cheap.
techs.what: Control when and how requests reach the model: queue them, merge identical requests already in flight, rate-limit per user, and move non-urgent work to quiet hours or cheaper service tiers.

techs.name: Batch Processing
techs.q: Can this wait a few hours for half the price?
techs.remember: Not urgent? Batch it and pay half.
techs.what: Submit large sets of non-urgent requests as one asynchronous batch.

techs.name: Semantic Response Caching
techs.q: Has someone already asked this, in other words?
techs.remember: Cache the shared answers, never the personal ones. Tune the threshold on near misses.
techs.what: Store whole answers keyed by the meaning of the question.

techs.name: Cost Attribution and Budget Guards
techs.q: Which feature, customer or run is spending the money, and what stops a runaway?
techs.remember: Tag every call; guard each run and each customer, not the whole account.
techs.what: The other techniques in this module lower the price of each call; this one makes spend visible and bounded.

techs.name: Semantic Embeddings
techs.q: Which texts mean the same thing?
techs.remember: Similar meaning, nearby vectors.
techs.what: An embedding model maps text to a dense vector, typically a few hundred to a few thousand numbers, so that texts with similar meaning land close together.

techs.name: Sparse Keyword Search (BM25)
techs.q: Which documents contain these exact words?
techs.remember: Exact words, rare terms, fast answers.
techs.what: BM25 is the classic ranking function behind most keyword search engines.

techs.name: Multimodal Embeddings
techs.q: Can one search cover text, images and more?
techs.remember: One space, many media.
techs.what: Multimodal models embed different kinds of content into one shared vector space, so a text query can find an image and an image can find related text.

techs.name: Contrastive Embeddings
techs.q: How do I make vectors fit my domain?
techs.remember: Pull matches in, push look-alikes out.
techs.what: Contrastive learning is how most embedding models are trained, and how you fine-tune one on your own data.

techs.name: Matryoshka, Quantised and Reduced Embeddings
techs.q: Can the vectors be smaller without losing recall?
techs.remember: Smaller vectors, measured recall.
techs.what: Shrink vectors to save memory, storage and search time.

techs.name: Multilingual and Code-Mixed Embeddings
techs.q: Can one search serve Hindi, Hinglish and English?
techs.remember: One space for every language. Normalise the script, measure each slice.
techs.what: A multilingual embedding model maps English, Hindi in Devanagari and Roman-script Hinglish into one vector space, so “when will my refund arrive”, “पैसा कब आएगा” and “paisa kab aayega” land near the same English article.

techs.name: Late Interaction and Multi-Vector (ColBERT, ColPali)
techs.q: Does one vector per passage lose too much detail?
techs.remember: Keep every token, match each one, compress the index.
techs.what: Instead of squeezing each passage into one vector, late-interaction models keep a vector for every token.

techs.name: IVFFlat Index
techs.q: Can I search only the nearest clusters?
techs.remember: Cluster first, probe a few.
techs.what: IVF (inverted file) indexing groups vectors into clusters with k-means, each represented by a centroid.

techs.name: HNSW Index
techs.q: Can I hop through a graph to the nearest neighbours?
techs.remember: Long hops on top, short hops at the bottom.
techs.what: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) builds a layered graph.

techs.name: DiskANN
techs.q: What if the index doesn’t fit in memory?
techs.remember: Graph on SSD, compressed copy in RAM.
techs.what: DiskANN, from Microsoft Research, stores a graph index (Vamana) and full-precision vectors on SSD and keeps only compressed vectors in RAM.

techs.name: Coarse-to-Fine Retrieval and Re-scoring
techs.q: Can a cheap pass narrow things down before a precise one?
techs.remember: Wide and cheap first, narrow and exact last.
techs.what: A multi-stage pattern.

techs.name: Hybrid Search
techs.q: How do I get meaning and exact matches together?
techs.remember: Dense for meaning, sparse for words, fuse by rank.
techs.what: Run dense (vector) and sparse (BM25) search side by side and fuse the two result lists, usually with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, which combines ranks rather than raw scores.

techs.name: Metadata Filtering
techs.q: Can I search by meaning and still respect hard facts?
techs.remember: Filter inside the search, index what you filter, test the rare filters.
techs.what: Combine vector similarity with structured conditions on each chunk, such as date, product, region, document type or version, so the top k are the nearest chunks that also match.

techs.name: Multi-Tenancy and Access Control
techs.q: Can one vector store keep every client’s data apart?
techs.remember: Tenant from the token, enforced by the database. ACLs in the query, synced on change.
techs.what: One vector store serves many customers (tenants) and many users, and every search must return only chunks the caller may see.

techs.name: Vector Compression (Scalar, Product and Binary Quantisation)
techs.q: Can the index fit in a fraction of the RAM?
techs.remember: Fewer bits in RAM, full vectors on disk, oversample and rescore.
techs.what: Vector compression stores fewer bits per dimension so a large index fits in RAM.

techs.name: Choosing a Vector Store
techs.q: Which vector database should we actually run?
techs.remember: Constraints first, two finalists, benchmark on your own queries.
techs.what: Choosing a vector store is a product decision, not an algorithm choice: the index types covered elsewhere in this module (IVF, HNSW, DiskANN) are available in most stores.

techs.name: Document Parsing and OCR
techs.q: Did the text, tables and layout survive ingestion?
techs.remember: Parse for structure, not just text.
techs.what: Turns PDFs, scans, slides and spreadsheets into clean text with its structure before anything is chunked or embedded.

techs.name: Chunking Strategies
techs.q: Does each retrieved piece hold the whole answer?
techs.remember: Cut along the document’s structure and carry its context.
techs.what: Splits parsed documents into the pieces that are embedded and retrieved.

techs.name: Query Rewriting and HyDE
techs.q: Can a model turn the question into a better search?
techs.remember: Fix the question before you search.
techs.what: Uses an LLM before retrieval to make the question searchable.

techs.name: Re-ranking with Cross-Encoders
techs.q: Are the best passages at the top, not just somewhere in the pool?
techs.remember: Retrieve wide, re-rank narrow.
techs.what: A second stage after retrieval.

techs.name: Citations and Grounded Answers
techs.q: Can every sentence in the answer be traced to a source?
techs.remember: No source, no sentence.
techs.what: Makes answers checkable.

techs.name: Agentic and Corrective RAG
techs.q: Should the agent plan, check and retry its own retrieval?
techs.remember: Plan the query, grade the results, retry or admit defeat.
techs.what: An agent plans retrieval instead of running one fixed search.

techs.name: GraphRAG
techs.q: Can retrieval answer questions about the whole corpus?
techs.remember: Extract, cluster, summarise; route only the hard questions to the graph.
techs.what: GraphRAG builds a knowledge graph from the documents before any question arrives.

techs.name: AST-Precise Localization
techs.q: Exactly which lines need to change?
techs.remember: Navigate by structure, edit by node.
techs.what: Instead of reading whole files or grepping text, the agent parses code into an abstract syntax tree and navigates by structure: the function, its callers, the class it belongs to.

techs.name: Speculative Decoding
techs.q: Can a small model draft tokens for the big one?
techs.remember: Draft fast, verify in one pass.
techs.what: A fast draft model proposes several tokens ahead.

techs.name: Prefix Caching
techs.q: Why recompute the same prompt start?
techs.remember: Same start, skip the prefill.
techs.what: Inside the inference server, the key–value (KV) cache for a prompt prefix is kept after a request finishes and reused by the next request that starts with the same tokens.

techs.name: Disaggregated Prefill
techs.q: Why make prefill and decode share a GPU?
techs.remember: Compute-heavy prefill, memory-heavy decode: split them.
techs.what: Inference has two phases with different needs.

techs.name: Agent Execution Graphs
techs.q: Which steps can run at the same time?
techs.remember: Parallel where independent, join where needed.
techs.what: Model the agent’s work as a directed acyclic graph of steps with explicit dependencies, instead of a strictly sequential loop.

techs.name: Latency Budgets and Streaming
techs.q: Where do the seconds go before users see anything?
techs.remember: Budget the p95, not the average. Show something early, wait on less.
techs.what: Set a user-facing budget for the whole request, such as first words within 3 s and the full answer within 5.5 s at p95, then measure p50 and p95 for every stage and change the shape of the request until it fits.

techs.name: Serving Engines and Continuous Batching
techs.q: How many requests can one GPU serve, and at what cost?
techs.remember: Continuous batching plus paged KV memory; size GPUs for p95 at peak.
techs.what: When you run open-weight models yourself, the serving engine decides how much work each GPU does.

techs.name: Quantisation for Inference (FP8, INT4, KV Cache)
techs.q: Can a big model run on fewer GPUs without losing quality?
techs.remember: Fewer bits, fewer GPUs; FP8 first, and measure on your own tasks.
techs.what: Quantisation stores a model’s weights, and sometimes its activations and KV cache, in fewer bits so it needs less GPU memory and moves less data per token.

techs.name: Workflow Patterns
techs.q: Do I need an agent at all?
techs.remember: Write the path down if you can. Let the model steer only where you can’t.
techs.what: Run the model along code paths you write: chains, routers and parallel calls.

techs.name: ReAct Loop
techs.q: What should I do next, given what I just saw?
techs.remember: Think, act, observe. Cap the loop.
techs.what: The model thinks, calls a tool, reads the result and decides again until done.

techs.name: Plan-and-Execute
techs.q: Can I plan the whole task before acting?
techs.remember: Plan once with the big model. Execute cheaply. Replan on failure.
techs.what: A planner writes all the steps up front; cheap executors run them; replan only on failure.

techs.name: Reflection and Evaluator–Optimizer
techs.q: Is this draft good enough, or should it go round again?
techs.remember: Critique against something real. Keep the best draft.
techs.what: A critic checks each draft against clear criteria and sends it back for revision.

techs.name: Search-Based Reasoning
techs.q: Should I try several paths before committing?
techs.remember: Branch when mistakes commit you. Prune with a good judge.
techs.what: Propose several thoughts per step, score them, and expand the best while pruning dead ends.

techs.name: Reasoning Models and Thinking Budgets
techs.q: How much should the model think before answering?
techs.remember: Spend thinking where the problem is hard, not everywhere.
techs.what: Let a reasoning model think before answering, with a budget set by task difficulty.

techs.name: Human-in-the-Loop Checkpoints
techs.q: Should a person approve this before it happens?
techs.remember: Pause before what you cannot undo. Save the state, show the evidence, resume cleanly.
techs.what: The agent pauses before risky actions; a person approves, edits or rejects, and the run resumes.

techs.name: Code as Action (CodeAct)
techs.q: Should the agent write code instead of calling tools one at a time?
techs.remember: Let it write code, but run the code in a box.
techs.what: The agent’s action is a short program rather than a single tool call.

techs.name: Function Calling Basics
techs.q: How does a model actually use a tool?
techs.remember: The model asks; your code runs. Match every result to its call id.
techs.what: The model returns a structured call to a named tool; your code runs it and returns the result under the same call id.

techs.name: Tool Interface Design
techs.q: Will the model use this tool well?
techs.remember: Design tools for the model that reads them, not for the API behind them.
techs.what: Treating a tool’s name, description, parameters, results and errors as a prompt the model reads every turn.

techs.name: Parallel and Sequential Tool Calls
techs.q: Which calls can go out together?
techs.remember: Sum becomes max, but only for calls that do not depend on each other.
techs.what: Running independent tool calls from one turn concurrently while dependent calls wait for their inputs.

techs.name: Retries, Timeouts and Idempotency
techs.q: Is it safe to try that again?
techs.remember: One action, one key, every retry.
techs.what: Timeouts, capped backoff with jitter, and one idempotency key per action so a retry never repeats a side effect.

techs.name: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
techs.q: How do I plug tools into any agent?
techs.remember: Write the server once; every MCP host can use it.
techs.what: An open JSON-RPC 2.0 protocol through which any host can discover and call a server’s tools, resources and prompts.

techs.name: Agent-to-Agent Protocols (A2A)
techs.q: How does my agent hand work to another agent?
techs.remember: Tools get calls. Agents get tasks.
techs.what: An open protocol for delegating a whole task to another agent, discovered through its Agent Card and tracked through task states.

techs.name: Tool Search and Large Tool Sets
techs.q: How does the agent find the right tool among hundreds?
techs.remember: Load a few, search for the rest. Descriptions are the index.
techs.what: Keep common tools loaded, defer the rest behind a search tool, and load only what matches.

techs.name: Tool Authentication and Scoped Permissions
techs.q: Whose credentials does each tool call carry, and for what?
techs.remember: Act as the user, only for this tool, only for a few minutes. Keep the key out of the prompt.
techs.what: Each tool call the agent makes reaches a real API with some credential.

techs.name: Agent Skills
techs.q: How do I give an agent many procedures without flooding its context?
techs.remember: Describe it well, load it late, script the exact parts.
techs.what: A skill is a folder with instructions, scripts and reference files for one kind of task.

techs.name: Context Budgeting
techs.q: What earns a place in the window?
techs.remember: Fewer, better tokens. Key facts at the edges.
techs.what: Treat the context window as a scarce attention budget: fill it with the smallest set of high-signal tokens that gets the task done.

techs.name: Short-Term Memory and Compaction
techs.q: How does the agent keep the thread?
techs.remember: Clear the bulk, summarize the rest, keep the IDs.
techs.what: Short-term memory is the working state of one session: messages, tool results and plans.

techs.name: Semantic Memory
techs.q: What does the agent know about this user?
techs.remember: Update, don’t append. Scope every search.
techs.what: Durable facts about users and entities, stored outside the model and carried across sessions.

techs.name: Episodic Memory
techs.q: Has the agent been here before?
techs.remember: Normalize the three scores. Inject lessons, not logs.
techs.what: Records of specific past experiences, such as a run, its steps, outcome and time, retrieved when a similar situation arises.

techs.name: Write and Forget Policies
techs.q: What should be saved, and when must it go?
techs.remember: Save less. Delete everywhere. Keep the proof.
techs.what: Rules for what becomes memory, how duplicates and conflicts are merged, and when memories expire.

techs.name: Agent-Managed Memory
techs.q: Should the agent decide what to remember?
techs.remember: Let it take notes. Check every path.
techs.what: Give the agent tools to view, write, search and edit its own memory, and let it decide when to use them.

techs.name: Procedural Memory
techs.q: Has the agent done this kind of task before?
techs.remember: Solve once, reuse many times.
techs.what: Procedural memory stores how to do things: workflows, scripts and skills distilled from past successful runs.

techs.name: Graph and Temporal Memory
techs.q: Can the agent remember who is linked to what, and since when?
techs.remember: Link the facts, date the links, close old ones.
techs.what: Stores memory as entities and relationships with time on every edge: who holds which account, who is nominee, which address was valid from when to when.

techs.name: Single vs Multi-Agent
techs.q: Should I split this across agents at all?
techs.remember: Split for breadth, not by default. Parallel saves minutes, not tokens.
techs.what: Split work across agents only when the pieces are independent and too big for one context, because multi-agent runs use about 15× the tokens of chat.

techs.name: Supervisor and Workers
techs.q: Who splits the job and puts it back together?
techs.remember: Brief fully, scope tightly, return summaries.
techs.what: An orchestrator splits a task, briefs isolated, tool-scoped workers and merges their short summaries.

techs.name: Handoffs
techs.q: Who should own the conversation now?
techs.remember: Distinct descriptions, typed payloads, capped hops.
techs.what: One agent transfers the live conversation to a specialist, who then answers the user directly.

techs.name: Shared State vs Message Passing
techs.q: How do agents know what the others found?
techs.remember: Type it, reduce it, scope it, source it.
techs.what: Agents share findings through a typed common store with reducers, or through structured messages, with scoped reads and provenance.

techs.name: Debate and Critic Ensembles
techs.q: Will more opinions make the answer more correct?
techs.remember: Vote first. Debate only if it beats the vote.
techs.what: Several agents answer independently, see each other’s reasoning and settle by vote or judge; plain voting often captures most of the gain.

techs.name: Failure Modes and Coordination Control
techs.q: Why did the team loop, stall or overspend?
techs.remember: Any cap stops it. Nothing counts as done until checked.
techs.what: Multi-agent teams loop, stall or stop early, so runs need OR-combined caps, a stop signal, repetition checks and a verifier.

techs.name: Parallel Sub-Agents with Isolated Context
techs.q: How do I run many pieces at once without flooding one context?
techs.remember: Fan out the independent, pass shared inputs in, bring back cards, check before merging.
techs.what: An orchestrator splits a job into independent pieces and starts one sub-agent per piece, all at the same time.

techs.name: OpenTelemetry GenAI Tracing
techs.q: Where did this run go wrong?
techs.remember: One span per step. Record what was served, not just what was asked.
techs.what: Record each run as spans with models, tokens and errors, then group failures to find the cause.

techs.name: Prompt and Model Versioning
techs.q: What exactly was running when it broke?
techs.remember: Pin the snapshot, label the prompt, stamp the trace.
techs.what: Version prompt, model snapshot, tools and parameters as one release you can roll back.

techs.name: Canary Releases and Prompt Flags
techs.q: How do I ship a change without betting all traffic on it?
techs.remember: Small slice, enough samples, widen only while guardrails hold.
techs.what: Send a change to a small slice of traffic and widen only while live metrics hold.

techs.name: Online Evals and Drift Alerts
techs.q: Is quality slipping on live traffic right now?
techs.remember: Check everything cheaply, judge a sample, alert on windows.
techs.what: Score live traffic with cheap checks and a sampled judge, and alert on drops and drift.

techs.name: Durable Execution and Checkpointing
techs.q: What happens when the process dies mid-task?
techs.remember: Record every step. Resume, don’t restart. Keys on side effects.
techs.what: Record every step so crashed or waiting workflows resume without repeating work.

techs.name: Timeouts, Circuit Breakers and Fallbacks
techs.q: What does the agent do when a provider slows down or fails?
techs.remember: Short timeouts, fail fast, always have a plan B.
techs.what: Timeouts, circuit breakers and fallbacks keep the agent up when a provider fails.

techs.name: Incident Response and Trace Replay
techs.q: The agent is misbehaving in production. What now?
techs.remember: Alert on money, contain before you debug, replay the exact trace, keep the failure as a test.
techs.what: When a live agent starts doing harm, you run a practised sequence: detect it from alerts rather than complaints, declare a severity and an owner, contain it with a kill switch or a rollback to the last good release, replay the exact failing trace offline to find the root cause, then turn the failure into an eval case and write a blameless post-mortem.

techs.name: User Feedback Loops and the Data Flywheel
techs.q: Are users telling us what is broken, and do we act on it?
techs.remember: Capture what users do, not only what they rate; triage weekly; turn patterns into evals and fixes.
techs.what: Users show whether an answer helped far more often through behaviour than through ratings.

techs.name: Threat Modelling for Agents
techs.q: What can go wrong, and where can it come in?
techs.remember: Private data, untrusted content, a way out: never all three unguarded.
techs.what: Map what the agent reads, does and sends, and break every lethal trifecta.

techs.name: Indirect Prompt Injection
techs.q: Can content the agent reads give it orders?
techs.remember: Content is data, not orders. Decide tools before reading it.
techs.what: Instructions hidden in documents, email or web pages can steer the agent; separate and confirm.

techs.name: Data Exfiltration Through Tools
techs.q: How could data leave, and who is on the other end?
techs.remember: Close the silent channels. Allowlist the rest. Shrink what can leak.
techs.what: Close the ways data can leave: rendered images, fetch tools, email; scope what can leak.

techs.name: MCP Tool Poisoning and Supply Chain
techs.q: Can I trust the tools my agent loads?
techs.remember: Tool descriptions are prompts. Pin them, hash them, scope them.
techs.what: Tool descriptions are prompts: vet, pin, hash and scope every MCP server.

techs.name: Sandboxing and Egress Control
techs.q: If the agent runs code, what can that code touch?
techs.remember: Treat generated code as hostile. Isolate, starve, allowlist.
techs.what: Run model-written code in isolation with no secrets, limits and an egress allowlist.

techs.name: Automated Red Teaming
techs.q: How do we find the holes before attackers do?
techs.remember: Attack yourself at scale, many ways. Keep every hit as a test.
techs.what: Attack your agent automatically across categories and strategies; keep every hit as a test.

techs.name: Agent Identity and Least Privilege
techs.q: Who is this agent, and what may it touch right now?
techs.remember: One agent, one identity. Carry the user too. Grant little, briefly, and log both.
techs.what: Every agent gets its own non-human identity, such as a SPIFFE ID, a cloud workload identity or a dedicated service account, instead of borrowing a shared admin account or a person’s login.

techs.name: Memory and Context Poisoning
techs.q: Can an attacker plant something the agent will remember and act on later?
techs.remember: Record where every memory came from; untrusted text never becomes an instruction.
techs.what: Prompt injection usually lasts one session.

techs.name: Secrets Handling for Agents
techs.q: Could the agent leak an API key or password?
techs.remember: The model never holds the key: broker it, keep it short-lived, scan everything.
techs.what: Agents call APIs and databases, so they need credentials, but anything in the model’s context can be repeated, logged or extracted by injection.

techs.name: System Prompt Design
techs.q: What does the model need to know before the first message?
techs.remember: Say who, what, rules with reasons, tools, format, and what to do when unsure.
techs.what: Brief the model in clear sections: role, rules with reasons, tools, format, and what to do when unsure.

techs.name: Few-Shot Examples
techs.q: Will examples help, or will the model copy them?
techs.remember: Few, diverse, balanced, shuffled. Measure per label.
techs.what: A few diverse, balanced, shuffled examples teach formats and boundaries without biasing the model.

techs.name: JSON Schema and Constrained Decoding
techs.q: Can I trust the shape of the output?
techs.remember: The schema guarantees the shape, not the truth.
techs.what: Strict structured outputs guarantee the shape of the output; values still need checking.

techs.name: Validation and Repair Loops
techs.q: What happens when the output is wrong?
techs.remember: Validate rules, return the exact error, retry twice, then hand over.
techs.what: Validate business rules, send the exact error back, retry at most twice, then hand over.

techs.name: Prompt Templates and Regression Tests
techs.q: How do I change a prompt without breaking it?
techs.remember: Prompts are code: templates, strict variables, tests in CI.
techs.what: Treat prompts as code: templates with strict variables and golden-case tests in CI.

techs.name: Prompting Reasoning Models
techs.q: How should I prompt a model that thinks before it answers?
techs.remember: Say what and why, not how. Ask for the answer, and match the effort to the task.
techs.what: Reasoning models, such as Claude with extended thinking, OpenAI’s reasoning models and Gemini’s thinking models, already work through a problem in their own thinking tokens before they answer.

techs.name: Long-Context Prompting
techs.q: How do I get reliable answers from a very long prompt?
techs.remember: Documents first, question last, quotes before answers.
techs.what: How to prompt when the input is hundreds of pages: documents first, each wrapped in tags with its source, the question and instructions last, and a request to quote the relevant passages before answering.

techs.name: Multilingual Prompting (Hindi, Hinglish)
techs.q: Will the prompt work when users write in Hindi or Hinglish?
techs.remember: English labels, the user’s language in replies, and test every slice.
techs.what: Prompts and structured outputs for users who write in Hindi, Hinglish in Roman script, or another Indian language.

techs.name: Prompt vs RAG vs Fine-Tune
techs.q: Should I change the prompt, the context or the weights?
techs.remember: Prompt for instructions, retrieve for facts, tune for behaviour.
techs.what: Change the prompt for missing instructions, add retrieval for facts, and fine-tune only for behaviour at volume.

techs.name: Supervised Fine-Tuning with LoRA and QLoRA
techs.q: How do I teach a model a skill or format cheaply?
techs.remember: Freeze the model, train a small adapter, hold out a test set.
techs.what: Train a small LoRA adapter on examples of the desired output, with a 4-bit base (QLoRA) when memory is tight.

techs.name: Preference Tuning with DPO
techs.q: How do I teach a model which answer is better?
techs.remember: Clean pairs, moderate beta, watch length and regressions.
techs.what: Train on chosen and rejected answer pairs so the model learns what reviewers prefer, without a reward model.

techs.name: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards
techs.q: Can I train on answers a program can check?
techs.remember: Reward what a program can check, and check the checker.
techs.what: Sample several answers, reward the ones a program verifies as correct (GRPO), and watch for reward hacking.

techs.name: Distillation into a Small Model
techs.q: Can a small model learn to do what the big one does?
techs.remember: Teacher answers, filtered; student tuned; traffic routed with a fallback.
techs.what: Tune a small student on a large teacher’s filtered answers and route most traffic to it, with the teacher as fallback.

techs.name: Evaluate Before and After Tuning
techs.q: Did tuning actually make it better, and what did it break?
techs.remember: Held out, deduplicated, big enough, and check what broke.
techs.what: Compare with the best baseline on a clean, large held-out set, and run general and safety suites for regressions.

techs.name: Training Data Curation and Synthetic Data
techs.q: Is my fine-tuning data clean, balanced and safe to train on?
techs.remember: Fewer, cleaner, balanced rows: dedup, decontaminate, fix labels, scrub PII, verify the synthetic ones.
techs.what: Curation builds the fine-tuning dataset itself: source examples from logs and experts, put them in one label set and one format, remove exact and near duplicates, fix wrong labels, balance intents and languages, scrub personal data, drop anything that overlaps the eval set, and fill thin intents with synthetic examples from a stronger model that are checked before use.

techs.name: Fine-Tuning for Tool Use and Agent Trajectories
techs.q: Can a small model learn to use our tools as well as a big one?
techs.remember: Whole trajectories, verified successes only, loss on assistant turns.
techs.what: General supervised fine-tuning teaches style and format; agent fine-tuning teaches a model to act.

techs.name: India’s DPDP Act and Rules
techs.q: What does Indian data-protection law require of my agent?
techs.remember: Say why, ask specifically, take less, protect it, delete it, report breaches fast.
techs.what: Notice, specific consent, minimal collection, safeguards and processor contracts, 72-hour breach reports, and erasure that reaches every store.

techs.name: RBI and SEBI Expectations for AI
techs.q: What will my financial regulator ask about our AI?
techs.remember: Inventory it, own it, test it, stop it, tell the customer.
techs.what: A board-approved policy, a risk-tiered inventory, validation even of vendor models, kill switches, human review and customer disclosure.

techs.name: EU AI Act Risk Tiers
techs.q: Does the EU AI Act apply to us, and at what tier?
techs.remember: Scope first, then tier, then role, then dates.
techs.what: Check whether EU residents are affected, classify the system by tier, identify your role, and plan from the dates.

techs.name: NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001
techs.q: How do we run AI governance as a system, not a scramble?
techs.remember: One control library, mapped many ways, audited on a schedule.
techs.what: Use NIST’s Govern, Map, Measure, Manage or a certifiable ISO/IEC 42001 system, with one control library mapped to every regulation.

techs.name: Audit Trails and Explainability
techs.q: Can we show exactly why the agent decided what it did?
techs.remember: Every decision replayable, every record tamper-evident, no raw personal data.
techs.what: Log inputs, versions, grounds, tool calls, reason codes and reviewers in tamper-evident storage, with personal data masked.

techs.name: Model and System Cards
techs.q: How do we document what the system is and where it fails?
techs.remember: What it is for, how well it works, for whom it fails, who to call.
techs.what: Document purpose, data, results by segment, limitations, oversight and versions, plus a plain summary for customers.

techs.name: Third-Party and Vendor Model Risk
techs.q: What happens to us when our model provider changes, leaks or goes down?
techs.remember: Read the terms, pin the version, test the fallback, write the exit, keep watching.
techs.what: When a bank or broker runs its agent on someone else’s model, the provider’s terms, versions and outages become the firm’s own risk, and regulators still hold the firm accountable.

techs.name: AI Incident Management and Reporting
techs.q: When an AI system causes harm, who decides, who is told, and by when?
techs.remember: Define it, grade it, log it, notify on the clock, fix the cause.
techs.what: Operational incident response restores service; AI incident management is the governance around it.

techs.name: Content Provenance and Synthetic-Media Labelling
techs.q: Can people tell that an image, video or voice was made by AI?
techs.remember: Label it, sign it, watermark it, and don’t let anyone strip it.
techs.what: Generative tools that produce realistic images, video or voice increasingly have to mark their output.

techs.name: A Plain SDK Loop
techs.q: Do I need a framework at all?
techs.remember: Start with the loop; adopt a framework for a need, not a trend.
techs.what: A 30-line tool loop on a provider SDK, with a step budget and an approval gate; you own everything else.

techs.name: Pydantic AI
techs.q: How do I get typed, validated agents with little ceremony?
techs.remember: Type the output, inject the dependencies, validate everything.
techs.what: Typed outputs, tools and dependencies over most providers, with durable execution through Temporal or DBOS.

techs.name: LangGraph
techs.q: How do I build long-running agents that pause, resume and survive crashes?
techs.remember: State per thread, a checkpoint per step, interrupt before risk.
techs.what: A graph over shared state with a checkpointer per thread, so runs pause for humans, survive crashes and resume.

techs.name: OpenAI Agents SDK
techs.q: How do I build agents that hand off to each other, with guardrails, quickly?
techs.remember: Triage, hand off, guard the edges, trace everything.
techs.what: Agents, handoffs, guardrails, sessions and tracing in a small package, best with OpenAI models.

techs.name: Claude Agent SDK
techs.q: How do I build an autonomous agent that works with files, code and tools?
techs.remember: A full harness: allow little, hook the risky calls, sandbox the rest.
techs.what: The Claude Code harness as a library: built-in tools, MCP, hooks, permissions and subagents, for Claude models.

techs.name: Google Agent Development Kit
techs.q: How do I compose agents and workflows across languages, especially on Google Cloud?
techs.remember: LLM agents inside workflow agents, in the language you already use.
techs.what: LLM agents composed with sequential, parallel and loop workflow agents, in five languages, with A2A.

techs.name: CrewAI, AutoGen and Microsoft Agent Framework
techs.q: When do I want a team of role-based agents?
techs.remember: Teams only for work that truly divides; mind the token bill.
techs.what: Role-based crews in CrewAI, or Microsoft Agent Framework for .NET; AutoGen is in maintenance mode.

techs.name: TypeScript Agents: Vercel AI SDK and Mastra
techs.q: How do I build agents in TypeScript, next to my web app?
techs.remember: Zod-typed tools, a step limit, stream to the UI; Mastra when runs must pause.
techs.what: Many product teams work in TypeScript, and their agents live inside Next.js or Node services.

techs.name: LlamaIndex
techs.q: How do I build agents that are mostly about my documents?
techs.remember: Documents in, query engines as tools, Context you can save.
techs.what: LlamaIndex started as a data framework for RAG and is strongest when an agent’s job is mostly about documents: readers for hundreds of sources, LlamaParse for complex PDFs, indexes and query engines that turn retrieval into a tool.

techs.name: Screen-Understanding GUI Agents
techs.q: Can an agent use an app the way a person does?
techs.remember: Look, act, look again; use an API when there is one.
techs.what: Screenshots in, clicks and keystrokes out, with a check after each step; for apps with no API.

techs.name: Browser Automation Agents
techs.q: Should the agent read the page or look at it?
techs.remember: Read the tree, script what is fixed, let the agent handle the rest.
techs.what: A controlled browser observed through the accessibility tree, with fixed steps scripted and the agent handling what varies.

techs.name: Realtime Voice Agents and Latency Budgets
techs.q: How fast must a voice agent answer, and in which language?
techs.remember: Stream everything, detect turns smartly, test on real callers.
techs.what: Reply within about 600–800 ms with streaming and smart turn detection, using speech models tested on real callers’ languages.

techs.name: Multimodal Inputs
techs.q: How should the agent read documents, images and screenshots?
techs.remember: Clean the image, read it twice, check the fields.
techs.what: Preprocess images, extract into a schema with a vision model, cross-check key fields and route disagreements to people.

techs.name: Safety for Agents that Act on Screens
techs.q: What stops a screen agent from doing damage?
techs.remember: Isolate, allowlist, never show secrets, confirm what cannot be undone.
techs.what: Sandbox, allowlist, vault-filled credentials, injection screening, confirmation of irreversible actions and full recording.

techs.name: Evaluating Computer-Use Agents
techs.q: How do we know it works, beyond a scoreboard?
techs.remember: Your tasks, your environment, several runs, adversarial cases.
techs.what: OSWorld and WebArena show capability; launch decisions need your own tasks, repeated runs and adversarial cases.

techs.name: Speech in Indian Languages
techs.q: Does the agent hear Hindi, Tamil and Hinglish correctly?
techs.remember: Measure per language on your own calls. Identify each turn, boost your words, read amounts back.
techs.what: Speech recognition and synthesis for Hindi, Tamil, Bengali and other Indian languages, including callers who switch between them and English mid-sentence.

techs.name: Telephony and Contact-Centre Integration
techs.q: How does a voice agent plug into real phone lines and a contact centre?
techs.remember: Stream the call close to the caller; transfer warm; respect the rules.
techs.what: A voice agent in a lab talks to a browser microphone; in production it must answer phone calls.

The same PII redaction that screens prompts should screen what is written to memory.

In an execution graph the steps are fixed in advance; a supervisor decides them at run time.
Per-worker tool scopes are least privilege applied to each agent.
Routing picks a model for one request; a handoff moves ownership of the conversation, with its state, to another agent.
Procedural memory is one agent’s store; shared state is about concurrent writes and read scopes across several agents.
LLM judges grade outputs after the fact; debate produces the answer at run time, and its judge step reuses the same rubric discipline.
Prompt and tool controls trim one agent’s usage; coordination control adds team-level caps on turns, tokens, time and depth.
The verifier that must pass before a team stops plays the agent-as-judge role.
System-level evals run offline before release; online evals keep scoring the same qualities on live traffic after it.

Durable workflows run activities at least once, so side-effecting activities still need idempotency keys.
Offline system-level evals are the gate before a canary; the canary is the last check on live traffic.
Token counts on every span show which steps and tools drive cost, the input for step caps and tool pruning.
A routed system has one release per route: pin the snapshot for each model tier and version them together.
Input rails screen what enters the prompt; indirect injection arrives through documents and tool results, so rails must cover those too, not just the chat box.
Output rails that strip untrusted links and images close the quietest exfiltration channel.
Zero-trust runtime controls are the mitigations a threat model assigns to each agent capability.

conn.an: MCP Tool Poisoning and Supply Chain
conn.note: MCP makes tools pluggable, and every server’s tool descriptions become prompt text the model trusts.
Sandboxes and egress allowlists are the enforcement layer of a zero-trust agent runtime.
A red-team suite is a security benchmark: rerun it on every release and track attack success like any eval.
Injected text written to long-term memory keeps attacking future sessions; memory write policies are a defence.
Run the red-team regression suite as a release gate before a canary starts.
Stable system-prompt text first and variables last is what makes prompt caching work.
Templates and regression tests make a prompt change safe to write; a registry and trace stamps make it safe to ship and roll back.
Strict tool use applies the same schema guarantee to tool arguments that structured outputs give to answers.
A repair loop is an output rail that fixes rather than blocks: validate, send the error back, and escalate if it still fails.
Few-shot examples in a judge prompt carry the same label and order biases, so calibrate judges on held-out labels.
A golden-case suite for prompts is a system-level eval run on every change.
A planner that returns a structured list of steps is far easier to execute and check than one that writes prose.
A distilled student is only useful behind a router: easy, common queries go to the student and hard or low-confidence ones to the teacher.
Before-and-after evaluation of a tuned model is a system-level eval on a clean held-out set, plus regression suites.
If the gap is knowledge rather than behaviour, fix retrieval and measure it with RAG evals before considering tuning.
Reasoning models are largely trained with reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards such as maths answers and passing tests.

conn.an: Supervised Fine-Tuning with LoRA and QLoRA
conn.note: Few-shot examples teach in the prompt on every call; fine-tuning bakes the same examples into the weights once, which pays off at high volume.
An LLM judge can label preference pairs at scale, but its biases, such as preferring longer answers, pass straight into DPO.
Offline evals decide whether a tuned model may ship; a canary on a slice of live traffic confirms it before full rollout.
Many format problems that seem to need fine-tuning are solved by strict structured outputs at no training cost.
Traces show how an agent behaved for engineers; an audit trail turns the same data into a tamper-evident decision record for auditors and regulators.
A DPDP erasure request must reach agent memory and embeddings, not just the main database.
Input rails that mask PII before the model sees it are a core DPDP safeguard.

conn.an: RBI and SEBI Expectations for AI
conn.note: Regulators’ kill switches and human-review expectations are enforced by runtime governance around every tool call.
A system card is only as honest as the evals behind it; report system-level results by segment.
Threat models and red-team results are evidence for NIST’s Map and Measure functions and for ISO/IEC 42001 risk assessment.
Each decision record should carry the model and prompt versions that the registry assigns.
High-risk systems need documented accuracy and robustness; before-and-after evaluation of tuned models supplies it.
A plain SDK loop is the ReAct pattern written by hand: reason, call a tool, observe, repeat.
LangGraph’s checkpointer is one way to get the durable execution that long agent runs need.

conn.an: CrewAI, AutoGen and Microsoft Agent Framework
conn.note: Choose a multi-agent framework only after checking that the work really needs several agents.
Agents SDK guardrails are one implementation of input and output rails, not a complete safety layer.
An agent with shell and file tools must run in a sandbox with narrow permissions.
ADK speaks A2A, so its agents can call and be called by agents built with other frameworks.
Pydantic AI’s output types are strict structured outputs with a validation-and-retry loop built in.
MCP lets tools written once be used from a plain loop or any framework, which reduces lock-in.

conn.an: Safety for Agents that Act on Screens
conn.note: Screens and web pages are untrusted content: indirect prompt injection is the main way a screen agent is hijacked.
OSWorld and WebArena are benchmark suites: useful for choosing, not a substitute for evals on your own tasks.
Extract documents into a strict schema so vision-model output can be validated and cross-checked.

conn.an: Realtime Voice Agents and Latency Budgets
conn.note: A fast, small model for the first reply keeps voice latency down; escalate hard turns to a larger one.
Playwright MCP exposes a browser to agents as tools that act on accessibility-tree references.
A computer-use agent is the ReAct loop with screenshots as observations and clicks as actions.

conn.an: Safety for Agents that Act on Screens
conn.bn: RBI and SEBI Expectations for AI
conn.note: Regulators expect kill switches and human review for high-impact actions; screen agents need both.

conn.an: Realtime Voice Agents and Latency Budgets
conn.note: Call recordings and transcripts are personal data: notice, retention and erasure apply.
Runtime governance limits what an agent may do; a human checkpoint is the step where a person decides the actions above those limits.
Approval decides whether an action runs; an idempotency key makes sure the approved action runs only once, even after retries.
A paused run is only as safe as its saved state: durable checkpointing lets it wait hours and survive deploys.

conn.bn: RBI and SEBI Expectations for AI
conn.note: Regulators expect human review of high-impact decisions; approval checkpoints with a decision log are how agents meet that.

When validation keeps failing on a small model, a cascade escalates that request to a larger one; tiering picks the cheapest model that passes each step.
Redaction with a short-lived vault is one practical way to honour DPDP purpose and retention duties.
Traces copy every prompt and tool result; redact before spans are exported, not only before the model call.
The input rail screens for attacks; personal data it finds is handed to redaction before the model sees it.
Data that was redacted before the model saw it cannot be exfiltrated by a hijacked agent.
Vision models read the pages ordinary parsing cannot: forms, charts and photographed documents.
Chunks are the unit that gets embedded; their size and context decide what an embedding can capture.
A cross-encoder is the last and most precise layer of coarse-to-fine retrieval.
Re-rank the fused hybrid list: fusion widens recall, re-ranking fixes the order.
RAG evaluation measures faithfulness across a test set; citations make it checkable in every answer.
Logging the cited sources shows auditors which document version an answer relied on.
Parsing is where personal data enters the index; redact it before chunks are embedded.

gloss: A2A
Agent2Agent, an open protocol for messages and tasks between separate agent systems.
acceptance rate
Share of drafted tokens the target model accepts in speculative decoding.
accessibility tree
A structured view of a page’s elements with roles, names and states, used by assistive technology.
ACL sync
Copying document permissions from the source system into the vector store’s metadata, nightly, hourly or on each change.
activity
In Temporal, a unit of work with I/O, such as a model or API call, run with timeouts and retries and recorded in history.
actor claim
The act claim in a token produced by OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693); it names the party acting on behalf of the subject, such as an agent acting for a customer.
adapter
The small set of trained weights added by LoRA; it can be saved, swapped or merged into the model.
adjudication
Settling each case where annotators disagree, usually by a senior reviewer, and updating the rubric where it was unclear.
agent
A system in which the model decides its own next steps and tool calls, rather than following a code path written in advance.
Agent Card
A JSON document an A2A agent publishes describing its identity, skills, capabilities and how to authenticate.
agent loop
Call the model with tools, run the tools it requests, return the results, and repeat until it answers.
agent skill
A packaged folder of instructions, scripts and references that an agent loads when a task matches its description.
AI incident
An event where an AI system’s development or use causes, or nearly causes, harm to people, property, rights or the environment.
AI inventory
A register of every AI use with owner, purpose, model, vendor and risk tier.
AI management system
ISO/IEC 42001’s term for the policies, processes and controls that govern AI across an organisation.
allow list
Only listed values are permitted; everything else is refused by default.
allowlist
The only domains or actions an agent is permitted to use.
ANN
Approximate nearest neighbour search: finds close vectors fast by accepting a small recall loss.
approval limit
A rule in code, such as a rupee amount, above which an action pauses for a person instead of running automatically.
aria snapshot
Playwright’s compact text view of the accessibility tree for part of a page.
artifact
An output an A2A task returns, such as a document, an estimate or a booking reference.
assistant-only loss
Training loss computed only on assistant turns, with user and tool turns masked.
AST
Abstract syntax tree: the structured parse of source code.
atomic claim
A single checkable fact extracted from a longer answer.
attack success rate
The share of attack attempts that achieve the attacker’s goal, usually measured per category.
AWQ
Activation-aware weight quantisation: a 4-bit weight-only method that protects the most important weights.
barge-in
The caller interrupting while the agent is speaking, and the agent stopping to listen.
batch API
An asynchronous API that processes many requests at a discount within a delivery window, often 24 hours.
beta (DPO)
How strongly the tuned model is kept close to the reference model during preference tuning.
bi-encoder
A model that embeds query and document separately; fast because document vectors are precomputed.
binary quantisation
Keeping only the sign of each dimension, one bit, and comparing vectors by Hamming distance.
blackboard
A shared store that several agents read from and write to, such as a typed graph state.
blameless post-mortem
A written review after an incident that records the timeline, impact, causes and owned actions, and looks for system fixes rather than people to blame.
BM25
A keyword ranking function using term frequency, IDF and document length.
Bradley–Terry model
A statistical model that turns pairwise win and loss counts into a ranking of strengths.
broker pattern
A trusted service that holds credentials and makes calls for the agent, returning only results.
C2PA
An open standard for signed Content Credentials that record how a media file was created and edited.
cache breakpoint
The point up to which a prompt is cached; everything before it must be identical.
cache hit rate
Share of input tokens served from the prompt cache instead of processed fresh.
cache invalidation
Removing or retiring cached entries when the content they were built from changes, instead of waiting for them to expire.
calibration set
Representative prompts used to set quantisation scales.
canary release
Sending a change to a small share of live traffic and comparing it with a control group before widening.
CAPA
Corrective and preventive action: the fix for an incident and the change that stops it recurring.
cascade
Trying a cheap model first and escalating to a stronger one only when a check fails.
cascaded voice pipeline
Speech-to-text, then an LLM, then text-to-speech, each streaming.
centroid
The average vector of a cluster; IVF compares queries with centroids first.
checkpointer
The component that saves an agent's state after each step so a paused or failed run can resume from where it stopped.
checkpointer
A component that saves an agent’s thread state by session ID so it can resume later.
checkpointer
LangGraph’s store that saves graph state after each step, per thread.
chunk
A passage a document is split into before embedding.
chunk overlap
Tokens repeated at the end of one chunk and the start of the next, so boundary sentences are not lost.
circuit breaker
A guard that stops calling a failing dependency for a while, then probes it before resuming.
citation verification
Checking in code that each cited span exists in its source and supports the claim.
classifier
A model that assigns a label and a score to text, such as a safety model that flags harmful requests.
CLIP
A model trained on image–caption pairs so text and images share one vector space.
code action
An agent step expressed as a short program that calls tools as functions, instead of a single structured tool call.
code-mixing
Switching between languages within one message, such as Hindi and English in Hinglish.
code-mixing
Switching between languages within a sentence, such as Hindi and English.
Cohen's κ
Agreement between two raters corrected for chance: 1 is perfect, 0 is chance level.
ColPali
A late-interaction model that embeds patches of page images, so documents can be searched without OCR.
community summary
An LLM-written report of a cluster of related entities in a GraphRAG index.
compaction
Summarizing older parts of a conversation into a shorter block so the session can continue within the window.
compounding error
When each step’s errors carry into the next, so end-to-end accuracy is roughly the product of step accuracies.
computer use
A model controlling a computer through screenshots and mouse and keyboard actions.
concentration risk
The risk that many critical services depend on one provider, so a single outage, price change or exit hits all of them at once.
concurrency cap
The maximum number of sub-agents or calls allowed to run at the same time, often enforced with a semaphore.
condensed return
The short, fixed-format result a sub-agent sends back, such as a card of at most 500 tokens, instead of its full transcript.
confident learning
A method that uses a model’s out-of-sample predicted probabilities to estimate which examples are probably mislabelled, so people review those first.
consent manager
A registered entity through which people give, manage and withdraw consent under the DPDP Rules.
constrained decoding
Restricting which tokens the model can generate so the output follows a grammar or schema.
contamination
Benchmark items leaking into a model's training data, inflating its score.
contamination
Test cases, or near-copies of them, appearing in the training data, which inflates scores.
context engineering
Choosing and arranging the tokens a model sees at each step: instructions, memories, history and tool results.
context isolation
Keeping each agent’s intermediate reading and tool calls out of other agents’ context windows.
context precision
Whether relevant chunks are ranked near the top of the retrieved list.
context recall
Share of the reference answer's facts covered by the retrieved context.
context rot
The drop in accuracy as input length grows, even when the task itself stays simple.
context window
The maximum number of tokens a model can consider in one request, including the prompt and its output.
context window
The maximum number of tokens a model can consider in one request.
contextual chunk header
The document title and section path prepended to a chunk before embedding.
continuous batching
Adding and removing requests from the running batch at every decoding step.
corrective RAG
A pattern that grades retrieved passages and rewrites the query, switches source or abstains when they are weak.
cosine distance
One minus cosine similarity; a distance threshold of 0.10 is the same as requiring similarity of at least 0.90.
cosine similarity
The cosine of the angle between two vectors: 1 means same direction, 0 unrelated.
cost attribution
Splitting spend by tags such as team, feature, customer and run.
crew
In CrewAI, a set of role-based agents working through tasks under a process.
critical path
The longest chain of calls that depend on each other; it sets the minimum wall-clock time.
critical path
The longest chain of dependent steps; it sets total latency.
cross-encoder
A model that reads query and document together to score relevance; accurate but slow.
cross-lingual retrieval
Search where the query and the document are in different languages, such as a Hindi question finding an English article.
custom vocabulary
Phrase hints or a trained lexicon that make a recogniser prefer domain words such as plan names and policy terms.
DAG
Directed acyclic graph: steps with one-way dependencies and no cycles.
data fiduciary
Under the DPDP Act, the organisation that decides why and how personal data is processed.
data flywheel
A loop where product use produces data that improves the product, which brings more use.
data principal
The person the personal data is about; a parent or guardian for a child.
data processor
An entity that processes personal data on a fiduciary’s behalf, such as a model vendor.
decode
Generating output one token at a time; limited by memory bandwidth.
deferred tool
A tool whose definition is sent with the request but hidden from the model until a tool search finds it.
degeneration of thought
An agent’s tendency to stick with its first answer even when it is wrong.
delegated token
An access token issued to an agent or app to act for one user, within the scopes that user consented to.
deny list
Listed values are refused; everything else is permitted.
dependency injection
Passing resources such as a database client into an agent run instead of using globals.
deterministic replay
Re-running a recorded agent trace offline with the same input, release and parameters, serving the recorded tool responses instead of calling live systems, to reproduce a failure safely.
distillation
Training a smaller student model on the outputs of a larger teacher model.
DLP
Data loss prevention: scanning outbound content for sensitive data such as account or ID numbers.
DPDP Act
India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, which includes duties to erase personal data on request or when its purpose ends.
DPO
Direct preference optimisation: training on chosen and rejected answer pairs without a separate reward model.
draft model
A small, fast model that proposes tokens for a larger model to verify.
drift
A change over time in inputs, outputs or quality compared with a reference period.
DTMF
Keypad tones pressed during a call, used for menus and entering numbers.
durable execution
Running a workflow so that each step’s result is recorded and the workflow resumes after crashes without redoing completed steps.
durable execution
Running long workflows so they survive crashes and resume from saved state.
dynamic credential
A credential created on demand with a short lease, such as a one-hour database user.
edge invalidation
Marking a relationship as no longer true by setting its end date, instead of deleting it.
ef_search
HNSW's query-time candidate list size; higher means better recall and slower queries.
effective context
The input length at which a model still performs well on your task, often far below the advertised maximum.
egress allowlist
A rule that lets outbound traffic reach only named, approved destinations.
embedding
A list of numbers representing text or an image so that similar meanings get nearby vectors.
episodic memory
Records of specific past runs or experiences, retrieved when a similar situation comes up.
evaluator–optimizer
A loop in which one call generates a draft and another evaluates it against criteria and returns feedback for revision.
exfiltration
Moving data out of a system to a place the attacker controls.
exit plan
A documented, rehearsed plan to move a service off a vendor: what moves, how it is tested, how data is returned and deleted, and how long it takes.
exponential backoff
Waiting longer after each failed attempt, for example 0.5 s, 1 s, 2 s, up to a cap.
exponential backoff
Retrying after increasing delays (1 s, 2 s, 4 s…) to avoid overloading a service.
failure pattern
A named, counted cluster of similar failures found during triage.
faithfulness
Share of an answer's claims supported by the retrieved context.
false flag
A correct answer wrongly marked as unsupported by a checker.
false hit
A semantic-cache match that returns a stored answer to a question it does not fit, such as a UAE roaming answer for a USA roaming question.
false positive
A safe item wrongly flagged or blocked.
fan-out and fan-in
Starting many independent pieces of work at once, then collecting and combining their results in one step.
feature flag

few-shot prompting
Including a few input–output examples in the prompt to show the model what to do.
filtered ANN

fine-tuning
Continuing to train a pretrained model on your own examples so its weights change.
FP8
An 8-bit floating-point format for weights and activations, supported on recent GPUs.
framework lock-in
Depending on a framework’s abstractions so deeply that switching is costly.

RBI’s Framework for Responsible and Ethical Enablement of AI (August 2025), with seven sutras and six pillars.

Choosing a random wait between zero and the backoff value, so clients do not retry in step.

golden set

grounding
